title: From Observation to Explanation: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM-Generated Code for Principled Repair
comment: This camera-ready version was accepted at the EASE 2026 doctoral symposium
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development, yet our understanding of how they generate code remains critically underdeveloped. We address this gap by triangulating evidence across three layers. Longitudinally, autonomous agent-attributed code is statistically indistinguishable from human code under a semantic modification definition (HR = 1.019, p = 0.490), yet attracts disproportionately corrective modifications in production (49.1% vs 37.9% human baseline). This finding demands a causal explanation. Empirically, existing benchmarks overestimate LLM capabilities: models that achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks attain only 24 to 35% on real-world class-level code. Behaviourally, detection systems reveal puzzling asymmetries: GPT-3.5 is far more detectable than modern models (AUC-ROC = 0.96, a 27-point gap), even though modern models produce mutually similar code structures; yet no single feature reliably distinguishes AI-generated from human code at the class level, and the leading commercial detector achieves only 15 to 64% recall. Together, these findings raise a question that empirical studies cannot answer: why do LLMs generate code with these properties? This thesis proposes mechanistic interpretability, a causal token-level circuit tracing, as the bridge between empirical observation and principled correction. By identifying the transformer circuits responsible for detectable stylistic signatures, hallucination patterns, and systematic defects, we aim to drive an agentic repair framework that intervenes at the causal source of defects rather than patching surface symptoms.

title: How Far Can LLMs Go in Generating Android Lint Checks from Natural Language?
comment: Accepted at ICSE 2027, Dublin, Ireland. 13 pages (11 pages plus 2 pages of references)
summary: Static analysis tools such as Android Lint, PMD, and CodeQL let developers add custom checks for project-specific rules. However, authoring a check is a demanding programming task: a rule can be stated in a few sentences, yet turning it into a working, tested check requires detailed knowledge of the analysis framework and its issue-detection logic. Recent work generates such checks with large language models (LLMs), but each system needs more than the natural language description a developer always has: a bug-fix patch, a CVE record, or a developer-written test suite to repair against. No prior work measures whether an LLM can turn a description into a working check, or what external knowledge it needs to do so. We introduce LintBench, a human-validated benchmark of 113 real-world Android Lint checks, each paired with a natural language description and its original test suite as a held-out oracle. We evaluate four LLMs, including proprietary and open-weight models. We compare prompting strategies, then evaluate execution-guided repair with and without retrieved API knowledge. Prompting alone reaches 30%-65% (pass@5) across models. Execution-guided repair and retrieval reach 57%-85% test-passing rates within five calls. Our results show that execution feedback raises the pass rate, while retrieved framework knowledge raises the compile rate, which reaches up to 99%. The framework knowledge helps the low-performing models the most, providing the knowledge they need to fix compilation errors. Of the generated checks that compile but fail their tests, 87% have false negatives, missing an issue the generated check should report. Based on our findings, getting the issue-detection logic right remains an open challenge. We release LintBench and the evaluation harness to support future work on generating Android Lint checks.

title: SecretSifter: A Runtime Secret-Detection Engine for Live Web Traffic
comment: Version of record, published open access in SoftwareX under CC BY 4.0. 16 pages
summary: Credentials embedded in client-delivered web artifacts, such as minified JavaScript bundles, webpack chunks, server-side-rendered state objects, and JSON or XML API responses, form a runtime attack surface that repository-time (shift-left) secret scanners do not observe, because the credential enters the served artifact at build time or at runtime, after every source-code gate has passed. This paper presents SecretSifter, an open-source runtime secret-detection engine that inspects live web traffic and reports secret-grade credentials at the point they are delivered to the browser. The engine combines format-anchored and context-gated detection rules, semantic key-name extraction, Shannon-entropy scoring, and dedicated detection of hardcoded CryptoJS/AES material across the full served surface. SecretSifter ships as three editions over one shared detection core: a Burp Suite extension, a Chrome extension, and a standalone Windows and macOS desktop application, with a Bearer-authenticated REST and MCP interface for automation. On a 198-value benchmark of real production client-exposed values (GT-198), the deterministic detection stage reached 79.8% recall at 86.8% precision in default configuration, the highest F1 of any system evaluated. The detection core is released under an open-source (MIT) license, and a de-identified reproducibility bundle and a public synthetic demo target are provided.

title: Jailbreaks Are Global or Regional? A Controlled Study of Scale and Geolocation Effects on LLM Safety Verification
summary: Safety tests are used to compare language models and to decide where they can be deployed. Their main number, the attack success rate (ASR), can only be compared across models if nothing but the model changes. We test two factors that are usually assumed away: the size of the model and the place a request seems to come from. We evaluate twelve models from 0.5B to 671B parameters with a paired two-phase protocol (plain harmful prompts, then the same requests inside published jailbreak templates). We also send identical prompts through VPN exit nodes in five cities on three continents. Inside the Llama and Qwen families, Phase~2 ASR falls steeply with size (Qwen2.5: 70.8\% at 0.5B, 51.2\% at 7B, 12.6\% at 72B). Wrapping shifts every model by a similar amount on the log-odds scale (1.7 to 2.9); small models shift slightly more, but that gap nearly vanishes when we allow for judge false positives. Parameter count is a weak proxy for safety: Phi-3.5-mini (3.8B) has less than half the ASR of Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B, and Mixtral-8x7B is far weaker than 70B dense models. Judge agreement falls as ASR rises ($r=-0.96$), so ASR gaps between sizes carry unequal measurement error; the size gap survives a stress test, but Phi-3.5-mini's lead does not. A small activation probe is consistent with Phi-3.5-mini keeping a clear refusal/compliance split under wrapping while Qwen2.5-0.5B loses it. We detect no effect of request location (permutation $p\ge0.18$ for three models). The test is limited: it could only detect a true between-city spread of about 2--5 points or a single-city shift of about 5--8 points, and most hosted models were reached through a gateway that may hide the exit city from the model provider. We close with a reporting checklist for safety verification.

title: SafeJIT: A Speculating JIT Engine Verified Down to the Machine Code
summary: JIT compilers are among the most attacked components of modern software. They compile attacker-chosen programs, speculate on attacker-influenced type feedback, and run the result at full native privilege. A single wrongly eliminated guard or a missing deoptimization becomes memory corruption. We present SafeJIT, a small JavaScript engine with a speculating baseline JIT, together with a machine-checked proof in Lean 4 that its statically linked RISC-V and x86-64 executables never crash, on any input, in a model of a Linux user process. The theorem is about the shipped binaries, executed instruction by instruction on Sail ISA models (for RISC-V, the official one), and it covers everything in them: the parser and bytecode compiler, the interpreter and its type-feedback recording, the JIT compiler, all machine code the JIT can generate for any program and any feedback (type guards, guard elimination, loop type facts, register allocation with deoptimization metadata, inline caches, deoptimization and on-stack replacement), a mark-sweep garbage collector, the runtime, and a freestanding libc. The C compiler, assembler and linker are not trusted, and neither is floating-point arithmetic. The proof uses separation logic (iris-lean) over a model of a Linux user process whose stuck states are exactly the ways a process can crash, including fetching code that has not been made executable or whose instruction cache has not been flushed.

title: Automated Safety Analysis for Agentic Workflows
comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at ICSE 2027, with appendices
summary: LLM applications are increasingly built as agentic workflows: programs that combine model calls, external tools, and control logic to act autonomously on a user's behalf. Because these workflows execute real-world actions, logical flaws in how a workflow is wired can cause severe harm in deployed systems. Unlike prompt injections or malformed API calls, these workflow bugs stem from defects in the workflow's design, yet no existing tool can statically validate workflow logic across frameworks prior to deployment. We present Apsis, a static safety analyzer that detects workflow bugs before deployment. To operate across frameworks, Apsis lifts framework-specific code into a common intermediate representation (IR). This IR models a workflow as a semantic graph of steps, data dependencies, and shared state, while annotating each component with behavioral properties such as whether an input is mandatory or how a shared channel merges concurrent writes. Building on this representation, we introduce a bug description language that formalizes recurring classes of agentic failures as declarative patterns over the IR. By matching these patterns against the IR, Apsis detects structural and behavioral flaws and pinpoints the exact step responsible for each bug. To evaluate Apsis, we construct, to our knowledge, the first corpus of workflow bugs, distilled from real-world reports across 13 widely used frameworks. On a reproducible benchmark suite drawn from this corpus, Apsis detects workflow bugs with 91% precision and 84% recall, and uncovers 36 previously unknown bugs in real-world workflows.

title: VAPY: Circuit Optimization with Backpropagation
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures
summary: Parameter sensitivities of analog circuits enable the use of gradient-based design optimization methods and unlock a range of sensitivity analyses. However, it remains a challenge to compute exact design parameter sensitivities for circuits that use PDKs, which use Verilog-A device models comprised of thousands of lines of code. Finite difference methods, which estimate gradients through simulation, require N + 1 to 2N simulations for each gradient depending on the method, which can become prohibitively expensive when many parameters are optimized. We present VAPY, a Verilog-A to JAX transpiler that compiles Verilog-A device models into autodifferentiable JAX code, enabling optimization with Circulax, a JAX-based circuit simulator. VAPY employs taint analysis to ensure only the necessary control-flow is rewritten with JAX-compatible calls, reducing control-flow overheads. We use VAPY and Circulax to optimize three analog circuits implemented in the SkyWater SKY130 PDK, which is built on the BSIM4 device model. VAPY-generated model gradients closely match finite-difference gradients, achieving comparable design quality in over 40X fewer circuit solves and up to 40% lower loss than Bayesian optimization.

title: Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities
comment: 25 pages
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.

title: An End-to-End Theory for Compositional Symbolic Execution: From Expressive Specifications to SMT (Extended Version)
summary: Compositional symbolic execution (CSE) is a powerful technique for program verification and bug-finding, yet existing formal theories of CSE do not sufficiently bridge the gap between idealised models and real-world tools. We present progress towards a foundational, realistic, end-to-end theory of CSE in the Rocq proof assistant. Our theory advances realism at both ends of the CSE pipeline: it supports an expressive frontend with algebraic data types, logical functions, and lemmas; it also provides a verified connection to SMT-LIB compliant SMT solvers. Our contributions include: (1) a CSE theory that captures practical verification patterns; (2) a standalone, reusable Rocq mechanisation of the SMT-LIB standard; (3) a proven-correct encoding from CSE backend queries to SMT-LIB queries that accounts for semantic discrepancies and optimises using type information; and (4) empirical evidence for the backend by extracting our verified SMT-LIB encoding and running it alongside the CSE tool Gillian's own encoding on a majority of its solver queries.

title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.

authors: Bruno Rucy Carneiro Alves de Lima
title: Cache the Knowledge, Not Just the Prompt: Dynamic Datalog as the Action Language for LLM Agents
comment: Accepted for publication at AICCC 26
summary: An LLM agent that answers questions about a knowledge graph writes a program per question, and its tools evaluate each from scratch. We give the agent a Datalog REPL, a session over a dynamic Datalog engine, in which rules are inserted and retracted like facts while derived facts stay current. Prompt caching reuses the model's processing of what a session shares, and the Datalog REPL reuses the evaluation of it. On chains of questions over three knowledge graphs, agents reuse a relation that the REPL keeps in 179 of 180 cases, with two models, and write fewer output tokens: SQL and Python agents write 23 to 82% more. With SQL tables or a Python namespace, Claude Haiku 5.5 stores almost nothing for later questions, and a chain of seven questions at 13 million facts takes it a median of 48 and 56 s, against 31 s with the REPL. Claude Opus 5.5 matches the REPL by storing tables in SQL, and when the data changes it stores views, which are evaluated again at every read. A relation that the REPL keeps is read like a table and stays current like a view. Datalog is a niche language beside SQL and Python, and with thinking enabled the models answer as accurately with it.

title: Dhaani: A Data-Flow-Driven Tool for Greenfield Construction and Brownfield Modernisation
comment: 4 pages, 4 figures
summary: Large language models can generate plausible code quickly, but an end-to-end prompt leaves developers with little control over decomposition, interfaces, or the assumptions that must survive later revisions. We present Dhaani, a free desktop application for greenfield program construction and brownfield repository modernisation. It makes an annotated data-flow diagram (ADFD) the inspectable contract between intent and implementation. In the greenfield workflow, Build, a user turns natural-language requirements into a typed graph, reviews process specifications and pre/post-conditions, ratifies generated modules, and proceeds in dependency order for Python or .NET (C#). In the brownfield workflow, Migrate uses source inference to recover an ADFD from a Fortran repository, performs target generation in bounded dependency groups, and exposes source-target alignment, generated code, errors, time, token use, and cost. The tool keeps code and artifacts on the user's machine and supports cloud or locally hosted models. Two scientific synthesis case studies produced executable systems where matched low/no-code baselines failed or were substantially less accurate. On 50 open-source Fortran repositories, the migration workflow made all 382 fixed source-oracle probes runnable and passed 327 (85.6%); two direct translation baselines each passed 83 (21.7% of planned probes). Pre-built installers and usage instructions are freely available. Tool and usage guide: https://shraddhasurana.github.io/dhaani/. Video: https://youtu.be/SShWwOMgJ9c.

title: What Field Enumeration Costs to Compile in C++26: Native Reflection, Structured-Binding Packs, Reflection Libraries and Hand-Written Serializers on GCC 16
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Code, raw per-run data and analysis scripts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24443567 (GitHub: https://github.com/DenysKachalenko/CPP26FieldEnumerationCompileCostArtifact)
summary: C++26 adds standard ways to enumerate a struct's fields, among them static reflection (P2996, with P3394 annotations) and structured-binding packs (P1061), alongside hand-written code, X-macros and libraries (Boost.PFR, reflect-cpp, Glaze) that now ship pre-C++26 and C++26 paths. We time each in a struct serializer with byte-identical output on GCC 16.2.0, at the front end and at -O2, in randomized interleaved rounds with code-level checks of every single-factor contrast. At the front end, inline native enumeration in the form used in several of P2996's own examples, an expansion statement over the std::span of define_static_array, costs about as much per struct of 16 scalar fields as Boost.PFR and 7.96x a P1061 pack, itself about as cheap as hand-written code. The same loop over a constant array costs 0.47x as much: about half of the span form's cost comes with the span. The ratio to P1061 shrinks on a heterogeneous type graph and at -O2. In a whole translation unit at the front end the library outweighs the mechanism: 200 structs take 0.59 s with inline native enumeration, 0.56 s with Boost.PFR and 3.86-4.13 s with the C++26 paths of reflect-cpp and Glaze, whose visitors also compute field names. Per type, each library's C++26 path is cheaper than its pre-C++26 path at 16 fields, but Glaze's gain reverses at 128 fields (pinned release v9.1.0); Boost.PFR's C++17 path grows almost quadratically with the number of types. Hand-written serializers sharing one overloaded name grow superlinearly with the number of types. The -freflection flag alone makes reflection-free code up to 1.264x costlier per type on GCC 16.2.0 and up to 2.578x on 16.1.0, so comparisons between mechanisms depend on the point release. Part of the span form's cost grows with the number of structs, which we trace to GCC registering block-scope statics in quadratic time (reported as GCC PR128928).

title: Micro Operational Robustness of LLMs on Code Generation
summary: It is now common practice in software development for large language models (LLMs) to be used to generate program code. It is desirable to evaluate the robustness of LLMs for this usage. This paper is concerned in particular with how sensitive LLMs are to variations in descriptions of the coding tasks. However, existing techniques for evaluating this robustness are unsuitable for code generation because the input data space of natural language (NL) descriptions is discrete and sparse. To address this problem, we propose a robustness evaluation method called scenario domain analysis, which aims to find the expected minimal change in the NL descriptions of coding tasks that would cause the LLMs to produce incorrect outputs. We have formally proved the theoretical properties of the method and also conducted extensive experiments to evaluate the robustness of four state-of-the-art LLMs: Gemini-pro, Codex, Llamma2 and Falcon 7B, and have found that we are able to rank these with confidence from best to worst. Moreover, we have also studied how robustness varies in different scenarios, including the variations with the topic of the coding task and with the complexity of its sample solution, and found that robustness is lower for more complex tasks and also lower for more advanced topics, such as multi-threading and data structures.

title: Ziv: A Language for Correctly Rounded Math Libraries
comment: 44 pages, 23 figures, 3 tables, including appendices
summary:
Developing performant, correctly rounded math libraries is challenging. Such implementations often rely on extended-precision arithmetic for correct rounding and precomputed constants for performance. Existing implementation languages, however, provide limited support for (i) high-level abstractions for such arithmetic and (ii) staged computation to combine precomputation and runtime computation in one program. As a result, existing implementations often miss abstraction opportunities and hard-code constants precomputed using separate programs. These practices make it difficult to write, understand, and modify these libraries.
  We present Ziv, a programming system for developing correctly rounded math libraries. It consists of a small language, a rich standard library, and a provably sound compiler targeting C. Ziv supports (i) high-level numerical abstractions via types and operations for extended-precision numbers, and (ii) staged computation via compile-time evaluation of expressions known to be input-independent. These features enable high-level code that unifies precomputation and runtime computation. We embed Ziv in Julia and evaluate it by reimplementing 19 functions from two state-of-the-art libraries targeting correct rounding; we achieve competitive performance with 2.63$\times$ reductions in lines of code. We also implement three new functions and automatically explore 824,256 variants, achieving 96.5$\times$ average speedup over an arbitrary-precision library.

title: "What Should I Do?" Guidelines for Responsibly Integrating AI in Software Engineering
summary: Speculations abound about the "right" ways for developers to integrate AI into their software engineering (SE) work, but the evidence that exists is sparse and contradictory. Yet, developers are held responsible for the products they ship with (or without) AI's help, so they need to integrate AI in responsible ways. To address this gap, we conducted a two-phase, large-scale investigation with 1,118 developers at Microsoft, GitHub, and Pfizer. In Phase 1, we surveyed 860 developers at Microsoft on where they sought and resisted AI support in their daily work, and from their accounts, synthesized 35 developer-facing guidelines: 29 across five categories of SE work and 6 cross-cutting ones. A year later, as AI capabilities and developers' experiences co-evolved, we validated them in Phase 2 with 258 developers in technology (Microsoft, GitHub) and biopharmaceutical (Pfizer) domains. Developers in our study found the guidelines clearly worded (92%) and relevant to their work (91%), and most wanted to adopt them in their own work (89%). We also report how developers described operationalizing these guidelines in practice: using AI to refine their craft and delegate verifiable work, while keeping judgment and accountability for themselves. For relationship-centric work, endorsement varied with developers' domain and their SE and AI experience. Overall, we offer concrete advice from in-the-trenches developers to other in-the-trenches developers, and a shared vocabulary that engineering teams can adopt to integrate AI well in their work.

title: How Far Can LLMs Go in Generating Android Lint Checks from Natural Language?
comment: Accepted at ICSE 2027, Dublin, Ireland. 13 pages (11 pages plus 2 pages of references)

title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
comment: 14 pages, 9 tables. Data and analysis code: https://github.com/CodeAssureLabs/external-feedback-coding-agents v2: adds a build and feature check of all scored repairs (Section 4.6); corrects the scoring of one pull request
summary: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).

title: SatMend: LLM Agents for Automated Software Repair in Satellite Constellations with Intermittent Ground Contact
summary: Satellite constellations rely on onboard software to sustain services across cooperating spacecraft. Maintaining this software requires handling related component versions and different failure causes while delivering repairs through intermittent ground contact. Automated software repair in satellite constellations remains underexplored, particularly the coordination of repairs across related versions with verified onboard recovery under intermittent ground contact. To address this gap, we propose SatMend, a software repair method driven by ground-based large language model (LLM) agents. SatMend organizes related versions into persistent sessions to retain diagnostic context and combines source and runtime evidence to select code repair or state recovery actions. It validates each version separately and submits ready candidates during continued repair, allowing ground preparation to overlap with onboard delivery and verification. Experimental results show that across configurations with 16 to 64 satellites, SatMend restores 192 of 224 faulty applications within 600 s, compared with 40 for SWE-agent, 77 for Agentless, 124 for RepairAgent, and 115 for SWE-Search. These results demonstrate SatMend's effectiveness in restoring applications and supporting service continuity in satellite constellations with intermittent ground contact.

title: Multi-Agent Coordinated Method-Level Refactoring of Rust Code
summary: As Rust codebases evolve, developers refactor code to reduce duplication, simplify complex methods, and keep related functionality together. Developers can make these changes manually or use IDE assists for supported operations, then check the resulting code with compiler diagnostics and tests. Method-level refactoring in Rust must preserve observable behavior while accounting for ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes. We present a large language model (LLM)-based workflow for extracting, inlining, and moving methods in Rust. The workflow combines candidate generation, configurable specialist review,and container-based validation. On six tasks from three open-source Rust projects, three end-to-end configurations passed all task checks on their first attempt, using 6, 13, and 31 model calls. To isolate the effect of review, we then gave four configurations the same six reference patches and six deliberately behavior-changing variants. A designated specialist rejected all six behavior-changing patches before container validation and let all six reference patches proceed, reducing Docker invocations from 24 to 12 relative to direct validation. The fixed specialist panel also caught all six faults early and rejected two reference patches over unmeasured performance concerns. On this workload, specialist review reduced execution work, while its effect on total time depended on review overhead and which patches reached validation.

title: fx(hash): Salvaging The Source Code of 28k Generative Artworks
summary: fx(hash), the most radically inclusive generative art NFT platform, went bankrupt and shut down on August 17, 2026. The ownership of its 2,705,350 artworks is immutable on the Tezos and Ethereum blockchains, but the source code that generates them is off-chain and in peril. We salvaged all 28,193 generative programs contributed by 5,532 international artists and archived them in Software Heritage. Here we explain why NFT generative art is fragile and the steps we took to salvage these software cultural landmarks.

title: AutoRPG: Harnessing Systematic AI for Non-Intrusive Low-Latency Mobile RPG Combat
summary: Automated combat in mobile RPGs plays a critical role in game quality assurance, requiring real-time behavior control that closely resembles human gameplay. However, existing approaches fail to satisfy these requirements, either because they lack fine-grained behavioral control or because they incur high inference latency. To address these challenges, we incorporate user gameplay experience to design AutoRPG, a systematic AI framework for automating mobile RPG combat. At a high level, AutoRPG decomposes the combat process into two stages: a high-level strategic planning phase that formulates the overall combat strategy, followed by a systematic execution phase powered by a suite of carefully designed lightweight modules encompassing target tracking, character movement, dodge maneuvering, and abnormal-state handling. Experiments on three popular mobile RPGs, i.e., Genshin Impact, Wuthering Waves, and Arknights: Endfield, demonstrate that AutoRPG consistently outperforms four competitive baselines across both combat quality and generalization capability, while behaving the most similarly to human players among all evaluated agents.

title: ReqSeek: Transformer-Based Automatic Requirements Identification for Building Large Requirements Datasets
comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM), 2026
summary: Large, diverse, and high-quality datasets are significant for advancing AI in requirements engineering, yet automated identification of requirements from Software Requirement Specifications (SRS) remains a challenge. Automatic Requirements Identification (ARI) methods demonstrate limited generalization to unseen documents across heterogeneous SRSs. This work presents ReqSeek, a transformer-based, domain-agnostic ARI model for recognizing ISO 29148-style requirements in SRS documents, supporting dataset construction. We curated the Automatic Requirements Identification Dataset (ARID), comprising 2,396 training instances from 23 heterogeneous SRSs, and fine-tuned four transformer architectures. RoBERTa was selected as the base model for ReqSeek and achieved 95% precision, recall, F1, and F0.89 on the held-out evaluation set. Exploratory human-model benchmarking showed performance comparable to humans while requiring substantially less prediction time than manual annotation. Post-hoc evaluation on out-of-domain (OoD) SRSs provided evidence of requirement identification beyond ARID. Robustness analysis demonstrated ReqSeek's insensitivity to minor linguistic variations while maintaining sensitivity to major ISO 29148-style violations. We applied ReqSeek to construct the Software Requirements Dataset (SwaRD), identifying 10,201 ISO 29148-style requirements from 231 industrial SRSs. SwaRD aligns with textual and semantic properties of human-curated datasets while exceeding them in scale and domain diversity. Our results suggest that transformer-based ARI can provide precise and generalizable requirements identification.

title: Admitted Is Not Effective: Lessons from a Notary-Gated Retrospective Loop in an Agentic Pipeline
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures
summary:
Agentic software development pipelines with frozen prompts can repeat the same mistakes across pull requests (PRs), yet ungoverned additions to instruction files grow without bound and do not generally improve task success. We present a retrospective loop for a four-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline in which a Retrospective agent proposes edits to learned rules every ten PRs and a Notary admits, merges, or rejects them while recording each decision in a provenance ledger. In a pre-registered study of 880 PRs on two Python repositories, the loop ran end to end and the Notary admitted 55 of 89 proposals, rejecting 8 that cited nonexistent evidence.
  However, held-out review comments and hidden-test resolution did not improve after ten retrospectives. Tracing each step of the loop, we found that sparse review signal (0.45 comments/PR) left little to learn from and that rules admitted on their stated evidence did not show measurable held-out effects. We derive six lessons and argue that governed loops should admit and retire every learned rule as a testable hypothesis.

title: Agentic Root Cause Reasoning and Localization of Unsoundness in Static Call Graph Analysis
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 8 listings, 1 table
summary: Static call graph tools cannot soundly model every dynamic language feature, yet rarely reveal when, where, or why their results are unsound. We present CGRizz, an agentic framework that diagnoses unsoundness for developers and warns users about it. During training, CGRizz compares static and dynamic call graphs to identify boundary edges: calls observed at runtime but missing from the static graph. For each edge, an LLM agent proposes a root cause, including the unmodeled program pattern and responsible tool location. CGRizz validates each proposal using three independent forms of evidence: runtime instrumentation detecting the pattern, a test case reproducing the missing edge, and a warning inserted at the implicated tool location. Validated reports help developers diagnose limitations, while the warnings form an instrumented build that flags potential unsoundness in new programs without dynamic analysis. We evaluate CGRizz on three benchmark suites using WALA, OPAL, and Soot. Of 1,459 boundary edges, CGRizz reasons about 10.3% directly, all confirmed by manual audit, and resolves another 84.1% by grouping edges with validated root causes. Tool maintainers confirmed several limitations, some of which have been fixed. The warnings flag 74%-92% of unsoundness in held-out programs. Guided by CGRizz reports, a coding agent refactored programs to remove 64% of targeted root-cause patterns while preserving functionality.

title: Can Vibe Coding Produce Accessible Websites: An Empirical Study on LLM Coding Agents and Skills
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly allow developers and non-professionals to create websites through natural-language instructions, with limited inspection of the generated source code. Although this ``vibe coding'' workflow lowers barriers to software creation, it may also propagate accessibility defects at scale. We investigate the accessibility of websites generated end-to-end by contemporary coding agents and whether agent-level accessibility interventions improve their output. We generated 90 websites for three projects using combinations of three coding agents, four language models, and multiple reasoning-effort levels. We evaluated complete interaction journeys using axe-core, IBM Equal Access Accessibility Checker, and QualWeb, and converged reports to observe violation prevalence and violated WCAG Success Criterion (SC). None of the 90 baseline websites was fully accessible, with an average of 80.43 violated interface elements. 13 WCAG SCs were violated at least once across the runs. Color contrast was the most prevalent issue, followed by labeling, semantic-structure, keyboard, and visualization failures. We reran 24 matched configurations with a general accessibility Skill and a contrast-specific Skill. Both significantly improved accessibility scores, but neither eliminated violations. User testing with blind individuals corroborated the experiential effects of the detected inaccessibilities. Moreover, functional correctness decreased with the inclusion of Skills. Our findings show that accessibility does not reliably emerge from vibe coding, and agentic interventions can both improve some accessibility issues and introduce new functional ones.

title: Landscape and Taxonomy of Prompt Engineering Patterns in Software Engineering
comment: Published in IEEE IT Professional, vol. 27, no. 1, pp. 41-49, 2025. Recipient of the IT Professional 2025 Best Paper Award. 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: Advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced their ability to handle ambiguous user instructions. However, effective prompt patterns remain crucial for usability and comprehension. This article presents a taxonomy of prompt engineering patterns for software engineering. It is based on a systematic literature review that was conducted in early 2023, when LLMs still faced significant limitations in context length and inference capabilities. Our study explores techniques that enhance the usability and reliability of LLMs, emphasizing the ongoing importance of well-designed prompts in optimizing task performance. Our findings highlight the critical role of prompt patterns in maximizing LLM's potential, even as their capabilities continue to evolve.

title: Context-Aware Proactive Self-Adaptation: A Two-Layer Model Predictive Control Approach
comment: Author's version of an article published in ACM Transactions on Autonomous and Adaptive Systems (TAAS), vol. 21, no. 2, Article 13, 2026. 36 pages
summary: In self-adaptive software systems, the role of context is paramount, especially for proactive self-adaptation. Current research, however, does not fully explore context's impact, for example on priorities of the requirements. To address this gap, we introduce a novel contextual goal model to capture these factors and their influence on the system. Using this, we propose a two-layer control mechanism with a context-aware model predictive control to achieve proactive adaptation for the software system and adaptation for the controller itself. By contextual prediction and a more accurate system model, our approach utilizes model predictive control to facilitate timely and efficient system adaptations, improving both performance and adaptability. Meanwhile, we perform requirement adaptation to update the contextual goal model, which in turn updates the objective function and constraints of the controller. Our experimental evaluations across two scenarios demonstrate the significant benefits of our approach in enhancing system performance.

title: Does the Agent's Map Match the Territory? Architectural Claims in AI Agent Context Files and Their Fit with the Code
summary: AI coding agents start every session without memory of how a system is built. Developers fill this gap with context files, such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. Agents treat these files as true, so it matters whether they match the code. We study two kinds of architectural claims that can be checked against a repository: path claims, which name folders and files, and dependency rules, which say what may import what. We check 41,090 path claims and 184 dependency rules from 3,602 context files in 3,346 open-source projects against the code and its history. About 5% of path claims point to paths we cannot find, but we estimate that only 2.2% are real errors, similar to READMEs (3.5%). When code moves, 61% of claims that became stale are fixed, most in the same commit. Dependency rules behave differently: 33 of 184 (18%) were confirmed broken on the day they were written, usually by older code, and nearly all stayed broken. Context files are good maps but less reliable rulebooks: their rules often describe the architecture a team wants, not the one it has. In an exploratory comparison of 7,480 commits, new rule breaks were rare. Agent-assisted commits broke rules about 1.8 times as often as other commits (0.29% vs. 0.16%), but with only 14 breaks this is not significant: an early signal, not evidence of a difference or of its absence. We used an LLM with human review at each step, and discuss what this offers and risks for mining studies.

title: LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration
summary: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.

title: STUN-Bench: Truly Unseen Tools for Evaluating Shared Tool Experience
summary: A tool router retrieves a few candidate tools per request and lets a language model choose. Methods that share experience across organizations add past requests about each tool to what the router retrieves. StableToolBench calls some of its test groups tests on "unseen" tools, yet the ToolBench instruction pool, which retrievers and experience-sharing methods learn from, contains every test query and labels every gold tool of the two single-tool groups among them. We release STUN-Bench (StableToolBench, Truly UNseen), a split whose experience pool has no item that labels or names 172 held-out tools. Unseen here means absent from shared experience and retriever training data, not from pretraining. On the split we find crowding: experience pooled from five simulated clients, added to an index of tool descriptions, outranks the descriptions of tools no client has used, which then often drop out of the candidate list. Under the Jina-v2 retriever, routing accuracy on held-out tools falls from 0.534 to 0.278. Retrievers trained for tool retrieval lose much less, and keeping experience in a separate index recovers most of the loss under Jina-v2. The split also reverses a conclusion: with every test tool labeled in the pool and our default leak filter applied, shared experience beats descriptions alone; on STUN-Bench it falls below them. The split, leak filter and evaluation harness are available at https://github.com/<org>/STUN-Bench.

title: AEGIS: Evidence-Guided Set Decisions for Requirement-to-Code Traceability
comment: Code, data, and supplementary material: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23944184
summary: Requirement-to-code traceability recovery identifies code artifacts that implement a requirement, but manual review costs limit how many candidates developers can inspect. Code relations can reveal candidates missed by textual retrieval, yet can also introduce code unrelated to the requirement. We propose AEGIS, which combines retrieval evidence and code relations to construct and revise trace sets under a project-wide review budget. Grouped retrieval and semantic retrieval supply candidates. A set objective combines relevance to the requirement with structural compatibility. Local search constructs sets of different sizes, and dynamic programming selects one set per requirement within the budget. Call-context admission then compares replacements using evidence from arguments and return values in calls involving protected members, while bounding retrieval-score loss. Across 13 projects, AEGIS achieves the highest project-macro average on nine of ten evaluation metrics among the compared methods. Relative to same-corpus adaptations of TAROT-VSM and FTLR+MC, it improves F$_1$@5 by 33.21% and 52.28%, and MAP by 38.58% and 49.08%, respectively.

title: Software-Engineering-as-an-Artifact: From Engines to Systems That Build Themselves
summary: Software engineering (SE) is evolving rapidly as generative AI and LLM-based agents grow more capable. Yet, as a community, we risk using these new tools to solve problems that a changing SE process may no longer pose. We consider how AI may transform, and in part already is transforming, both the SE process and the systems it produces. Drawing on scenario planning methods from futures studies, we extrapolate from observed trends to a deliberately extreme scenario in which the SE process fully materializes in artifacts (like context documentation and executable skills). Such a process would culminate in SE engines that autonomously produce and update systems directly from requirements and user requests. The work of human engineers would then shift from the product to the process: they would maintain the artifacts of these engines, while the engines produce and evolve the software. We probe this scenario in scenario-validation interviews with four SE industry practitioners. The interviewees found the scenario largely plausible and desirable, and two reported that parts of industry are already moving this way; one questioned whether tacit engineering knowledge can ever be fully captured in artifacts. Even if this end state is reached only in part, we argue that reasoning about it can inform the intermediate stages. SE research should therefore take such futures into account when choosing its research directions.

title: RepoClean: Evaluating Coding Agents on Repository-Level Obsolete Code Cleanup
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong repository-level programming capabilities. However, as software evolves, repository code may become redundant or obsolete, increasing maintenance costs and potentially introducing functional issues. Agents must therefore identify and remove unnecessary code safely, yet autonomous repository-level code cleanup remains insufficiently evaluated in isolation. To evaluate this capability, we introduce RepoClean, a benchmark of 200 cleanup tasks from 34 popular open-source Python repositories. RepoClean is constructed by automatically reintroducing deleted code from real repository histories into newer versions, preserving current implementations and retaining instances where previously passing tests consequently fail. To restore existing functionality without new feature development, agents must use repository interfaces and cross-file dependencies to determine which historical code to remove and which implementations to preserve. Evaluation of seven models shows that even the best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra, resolves only 23% of tasks. Further analysis reveals that agents remove substantially less obsolete code when cleanup is not explicitly requested. RepoClean provides a foundation for systematically studying these cleanup challenges and advancing coding agents toward autonomous software maintenance.

title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
comment: 47 pages. Preregistered at https://osf.io/ms7ef. Harness, trial records and analysis scripts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24445015 and https://github.com/libredb/agent-blast-radius
summary: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB). 12 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Leaderboard: https://surgehq.ai/benchmarks/sudo-l7
summary: Coding agents can now turn a well-specified ticket into a patch that passes its tests. Experienced engineers also notice risks the request never mentioned, question flawed premises, reuse what already exists and say plainly what they did and did not check. We present sudo L7, a benchmark of 60 software-engineering tasks written by staff-level engineers, mostly in private production codebases and each built around a place where a frontier model failed. A task pairs a realistic, underspecified request with a hidden, expert-authored rubric of atomic criteria (1,287 in all), tagged with eight behavioral dimensions from functional correctness to truthful reporting. An agentic grader reads the agent's transcript, inspects and runs its code, and treats test output as evidence. An attempt passes only if it meets every criterion of the two highest severities, and more than half of these gating criteria test something other than functional correctness. On the public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in its developer's harness or in OpenCode, three attempts per task), Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra pass 31-34%, and the other 13 models at most 18.9%. In a human-label study, three candidate model graders each agreed with a software engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts, about as often as two engineers agreed with each other. Cases from the benchmark show how one unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt and illustrate two sides of engineering judgment: flagging hidden hazards and avoiding needless work.

title: Improving Repair Agents with Cause-Chain Diagnoses
summary:
Repair agents resolve a growing share of real-world issues. Starting with the same information as a developer reading a bug report, they have to find out how the program fails before actually fixing it.
  We present FORECAST, which provides repair agents with a diagnosis of the failure. From the executions of passing and failing tests, FORECAST infers a cause chain, a short sequence of execution features, such as conditions or data flow, that explains how the failing runs diverge. FORECAST appends this cause chain to the issue an agent receives. It thus works with any agent that builds its prompts from the issue, without modifying the agent.
  We evaluate FORECAST on all 300 issues of SWE-bench Lite with five repair agents and two models, the commercial Claude Haiku 4.5 and the open-weight Qwen3.5. With the cause-chain diagnosis, every agent resolves significantly more issues. Over all agents, the share of resolved issues rises from 48.5% to 70.9% for Haiku 4.5 and from 31.2% to 56.1% for Qwen3.5. The open-weight model with the diagnosis thus surpasses the commercial model without it. The gains persist across repeated runs and for agents that already run the tests the diagnosis is derived from.

title: ReproShift: Cross-Version Adaptation of Linux Kernel Fuzzing Crash Reproducers
summary: Reliable crash reproduction is essential for diagnosing and repairing kernel crashes. Historical crash reproducers preserve concrete bug-triggering knowledge and can be reused for regression testing, bug revalidation, and impact analysis across kernel versions. However, kernel evolution can invalidate these reproducers by changing kernel interfaces, configurations, and execution paths. Migrating them is therefore challenging: the adapted reproducer must identify and modify version-sensitive behavior while preserving the bug-triggering operations and resource dependencies that define the original crash. To address this challenge, we propose ReproShift, an automated framework for cross-version crash reproducer migration by preserving bug-triggering semantics while adapting only version-sensitive behavior. Given source crash artifacts, a source crash reproducer, and a target kernel, ReproShift produces a migrated crash reproducer with same-bug validation evidence. Specifically, ReproShift first constructs a structured source-to-target context to identify migration-relevant kernel changes. It then performs constrained target-aware adaptation to revise version-sensitive reproducer operations while preserving the original trigger logic. Finally, it executes the adapted candidates on the target kernel and uses execution feedback and case-specific crash evidence to iteratively validate candidates and refine subsequent migrations. In a real-world deployment on an evolving upstream kernel, ReproShift further produces 22 upstream crash reports generated from adapted candidates, of which 7 have been fixed and 5 have received explicit maintainer confirmation. To systematically quantify its migration effectiveness, we construct a benchmark of 107 real-world source-target migration cases. ReproShift achieves confirmed same-bug migration in 57 cases, compared with 19 cases using direct replay.

title: Interrupt-Aware Static Detection of Deadlocks in Rust Operating Systems
summary: Rust is increasingly adopted in operating systems, but Rust's safety guarantees do not eliminate deadlocks, especially those induced by interrupts. The core challenge is to recover interrupt-sensitive lock dependencies from Rust's guard-based synchronization across function boundaries. Applying this analysis across Rust OS projects also requires specifying project-specific synchronization semantics. We present an approach combining interrupt-aware static analysis with diagnostic-guided agent auditing for detecting deadlocks in Rust operating systems. Our approach uses lightweight source-level annotations to recover project-specific lock and interrupt semantics, performs a flow-sensitive MIR-based analysis to track lock-holding and interrupt states, and reports potential deadlocks with supporting evidence. An agent then searches for relevant source code in the repository and returns a confidence assessment with reasons for each supplied report. We evaluate our tool on four real Rust operating systems, identifying 26 true cases corresponding to nine maintainer-confirmed defects. Diagnostic-guided auditing achieves 86.2\% precision and 96.2\% recall based on static analysis results, and offers advantages over the baselines in both cost and effectiveness.

title: Useful but Unwieldy: How Software Engineers Perceive the Design of Chain-of-Thought Explanations in Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents (CAs) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. As these CAs take up more tasks and responsibilities, it is imperative for software engineers to understand the CA's rationale behind its' decisions, also known as the chain-of-thought (CoT). During the interaction, some CAs are capable of showing this CoT as a separate message to users with the goal of providing transparency and explainability. However, its effectiveness as an explainable AI (XAI) mechanism for end-users in software engineering has not yet been established in the literature. This motivates us to understand their experiences with the CoT message as an XAI tool through a survey and semi-structured follow-up interviews with 36 software engineers. Through thematic analysis of the survey responses and interview transcripts, we found that CoT message is an indispensable tool for software engineers in terms of transparency, scrutability, and trust towards the CA. However, various instances of CoT messages being overly verbose, containing technical information that does not match the users' expertise, or being perceived by the users as ``detached'' from the conversation because the ``agent is talking to itself'', lead to comprehension difficulties and selective use or abandonment of the tool. We synthesize these insights to inform the design of CoT messages that support software engineers in their explainability needs.

title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
summary: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as \emph{personal software}. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

title: What Field Enumeration Costs to Compile in C++26: Native Reflection, Structured-Binding Packs, Reflection Libraries and Hand-Written Serializers on GCC 16
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables. Code, raw per-run data and analysis scripts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24443567 (GitHub: https://github.com/DenysKachalenko/CPP26FieldEnumerationCompileCostArtifact)
summary: C++26 adds standard ways to enumerate a struct's fields, among them static reflection (P2996, with P3394 annotations) and structured-binding packs (P1061), alongside hand-written code, X-macros and libraries (Boost.PFR, reflect-cpp, Glaze) that now ship pre-C++26 and C++26 paths. We time each in a struct serializer with byte-identical output on GCC 16.2.0, at the front end and at -O2, in randomized interleaved rounds with code-level checks of every single-factor contrast. At the front end, inline native enumeration in the form used in several of P2996's own examples, an expansion statement over the std::span of define_static_array, costs about as much per struct of 16 scalar fields as Boost.PFR and 7.96x a P1061 pack, itself about as cheap as hand-written code. The same loop over a constant array costs 0.47x as much: about half of the span form's cost comes with the span. The ratio to P1061 shrinks on a heterogeneous type graph and at -O2. In a whole translation unit at the front end the library outweighs the mechanism: 200 structs take 0.59 s with inline native enumeration, 0.56 s with Boost.PFR and 3.86-4.13 s with the C++26 paths of reflect-cpp and Glaze, whose visitors also compute field names. Per type, each library's C++26 path is cheaper than its pre-C++26 path at 16 fields, but Glaze's gain reverses at 128 fields (pinned release v9.1.0); Boost.PFR's C++17 path grows almost quadratically with the number of types. Hand-written serializers sharing one overloaded name grow superlinearly with the number of types. The -freflection flag alone makes reflection-free code up to 1.264x costlier per type on GCC 16.2.0 and up to 2.578x on 16.1.0, so comparisons between mechanisms depend on the point release. Part of the span form's cost grows with the number of structs, which we trace to GCC registering block-scope statics in quadratic time (reported as GCC PR128928).
